newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA STILL PAYING FOR DISMANTLED NUCLEAR BOMBS.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA STILL PAYING FOR DISMANTLED NUCLEAR BOMBS.

text.p: Nearly five years after it dismantled its six atomic bombs, the South African government is still making hefty repayments for loans taken out during the apartheid era to develop the nuclear devices.

Mineral and Energy Affairs deputy director general Jan Bredell clearly floored committee members of the National Council of Provinces on Wednesday when he told them that the Atomic Energy Corporation (AEC) would have to pay off maturing loans of 231.2 million rand.
This was more than a quarter of the ministry's 807 million rand budget at a time of general fiscal restraint as government battled to meet its deficit cutting targets.
"This relates to the special programme that the previous government had in the making of atomic weapons," he said.
"There was a time in history when the budget of the AEC was in the order of a billion rand a year but its operating budget is now down to about 200 million rand.

"But over and above that, the former government made commitments as far as loans are concerned...from international banks. This was an unfortunate period of the past but it is unfortunately also a financial commitment that we have to honour to get this thing past us, get it paid and over and done with.
The AEC's "2000" programme aimed to drastically reduce its dependence on state support by the year 2000.
"The AEC is undergoing a massive transformation where they have moved away completely from the manufacture of nuclear fuels, for example," he said.
The AEC was now instead using its expertise to produce high technology products for commercial use and was landing lucrative international contracts, Bredell said.

Former State President F.W. de Klerk announced in 1993 ahead of the country's 1994 all-race elections that the six nuclear devices had been dismantled and South Africa has since signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
